requirement:
The reviewer MUST assess the named subject using its text, referenced requirements,
and terminology definitions. For a requirement, the reviewer MUST assess whether
the code marked with `{impl}` implements every stated obligation completely and
exactly as stated, and whether its
tests cover the interesting cases in the design space, including relevant
boundaries and failure cases. The reviewer MUST also assess whether the
implementation is marked completely: code that implements part of the
requirement under {cite}`requirements.references.targets` without an `{impl}`
reference to it, including code that refers to it only with `{cite}`, MUST be
treated as a gap. Behavior in the `{impl}` code that the requirement does not
specify MUST be accounted for by another definition that the same code
implements; otherwise it MUST be treated as a gap. When another requirement implements part of the subject, the
reviewer MUST assess whether its text carries out that part, and MUST NOT
reassess its implementation, tests, or evidence; that requirement is assessed
separately. When there are no tests, the reviewer MUST assess whether the logic is
simple enough to need no test or a test is impractical to author, and explain that
judgment in the rationale.

For an example, the reviewer MUST assess whether tests exist whose setup and
assertions cover its scenario and expected outcomes. The rationale MUST identify
the relevant sources and explain the implementation and testing judgments for a
requirement, or the test coverage for an example. Referenced requirements provide
context; they MUST NOT become additional subjects to assess in full.
rationale:
**Judgment: `requirements.ci.review_criteria` is satisfied.**

**What the requirement asks.** It specifies the criteria a reviewer applies. The reviewer's instructions are the initial prompt. `requirements.authoring.initial_prompt` says the prompt's "review guidance MUST follow {impl}`requirements.ci.review_criteria`".

**Implementation**
- `md/requirements/authoring.md` (the `initial_prompt` requirement, line 524) carries the `{impl}` for this requirement. Its prompt template carries out each obligation:
  - **Assess the subject with its context.** "Assess only the named subject, using cited requirements and definitions as context." This covers the MUST NOT about turning referenced requirements into full subjects.
  - **Code and tests for a requirement.** The prompt asks whether `{impl}` code implements "every obligation completely and exactly as stated". It also asks whether "tests cover the interesting points in the design space, including relevant boundaries and failure cases".
  - **Complete marking.** Code that implements part of the requirement without `{impl}` is a gap, including code that only has `{cite}`. Behavior in the `{impl}` code that the requirement does not specify is also a gap, unless another definition that the code implements specifies it.
  - **Other requirements that implement part of the subject.** The prompt says to "assess whether its text carries out that part; do not reassess its implementation, tests, or evidence".
  - **No tests.** The prompt asks whether "simplicity or impracticality justifies their absence".
  - **Examples.** The prompt asks whether "test setup and assertions cover its scenario and expected outcomes", and says to "Explain the coverage".
  - **Rationale.** The prompt asks for "source locations" and, for a requirement, the implementation and testing judgments.
- `src/authoring/mod.rs` `fn initial_prompt` (lines 655–686) carries the `{impl}`. It loads the approved template from the authoring chapter with `prompt_template`, which uses `include_str!` on `authoring.md`. It then fills `subject_kind`, `subject_name` and `mandatory_inputs`. The criteria text therefore comes from a single source. The function also performs the citation-prompt branch and other duties, and each of those has its own `{impl}` markers for other definitions, so nothing it does is unaccounted for.
- The other sites that mention this requirement (`md/reference.md`, `ci.md`, `cli.md` and `examples.md`) are `{cite}` only. They do not implement part of it.

**Tests**
- `src/authoring/mod.rs`, `initial_prompt_carries_the_review_criteria`, builds a real prompt for a requirement subject. It asserts that the prompt contains each criterion:
  - the subject line and "Assess only the named subject";
  - "implements every obligation completely and exactly as stated";
  - the tests-cover-design-space wording, with boundaries and failure cases;
  - the rule not to reassess another requirement's implementation, tests, or evidence;
  - the `{cite}`-only and unspecified-behavior gaps;
  - the no-tests simplicity/impracticality judgment;
  - the example-coverage criterion;
  - "with source locations", the requirement-rationale wording, and "Explain the coverage".
- `tests/authoring_cli.rs`, `ollama_cli_delivers_sources_records_fixme_and_keeps_usage_content_free`, checks end to end that the prompt reaching the model contains the opening line, the requirement text and the "submit_judgment exactly once" instruction. That test is broad and only loosely tied to this requirement, but it adds coverage.
- The behavior is a fixed text template, so the design space has no meaningful boundaries or failure cases beyond verifying the text is delivered. The tests are proportionate to that.

**Gaps.** I found no unmarked implementation and no unaccounted behavior. There are no FIXMEs.

and terminology definitions. For a requirement, the reviewer MUST assess whether
the code marked with `{impl}` implements every stated obligation completely and
exactly as stated, and whether its
tests cover the interesting cases in the design space, including relevant
boundaries and failure cases. The reviewer MUST also assess whether the
implementation is marked completely: code that implements part of the

reference to it, including code that refers to it only with `{cite}`, MUST be

specify MUST be accounted for by another definition that the same code
implements; otherwise it MUST be treated as a gap. When another requirement implements part of the subject, the
reviewer MUST assess whether its text carries out that part, and MUST NOT
reassess its implementation, tests, or evidence; that requirement is assessed

For an example, the reviewer MUST assess whether tests exist whose setup and

requirement, or the test coverage for an example. Referenced requirements provide
context; they MUST NOT become additional subjects to assess in full.
:::{req} targets

Project text files MAY use the `{impl}`, `{cite}`, and `{test}` roles with a backtick-delimited full requirement or example name, or with a built-in name under {cite}`requirements.references.builtin_definitions`. A reference MAY instead be written in fenced form, `:::{role} name` on one line, a body, and a closing fence, following the fence rules of {cite}`requirements.ci.span` and {cite}`requirements.ci.fence_lengths`; the fenced form is the same edge with attached commentary, and the inline form carries none. In a source comment, fence lines MUST be recognized after removing each line's comment delimiters within one comment run under {cite}`requirements.references.outline_comments`, and a fence that does not close within its comment run MUST be a validation error. Each reference is a directed edge between its source and the named definition. A source is a project source item or a requirement or example declaration. `{cite}` MUST mean that the source relies on, supports, or refers to the definition, and is an edge from the source to the definition. `{impl}` MUST mean that the source implements part of the definition: it makes a decision, performs a check, produces an output, or handles a case that the definition specifies. A requirement MAY implement part of another requirement by refining one of its obligations. Calling code that implements a definition, or producing a result a caller uses to meet it, MUST NOT by itself count as implementing it. A requirement stating a convention for every output of a kind, such as every validation error, is implemented by the source that carries out the convention as a whole, such as the step that collects and reports those outputs. `{test}` MUST mean that the source is designed to verify behavior the definition specifies: a test through its scenario and the assertions about that scenario's outcome, or a named example through the concrete case it describes. `{impl}` and `{test}` are edges from the definition to the source. Only requirements and examples are assessed; code is reviewed as part of the definitions it implements or tests. Habeas MUST find these references throughout project source files and MUST fail with the source file and line if a name has no matching `{req}` or `{example}` definition. In Markdown, escaped roles and roles in code examples MUST remain literal. Reference discovery MUST consider exactly the project sources that source-access policy permits under {cite}`requirements.authoring.source_tools`: in a Git worktree, files present in the Git index, including staged new files; outside Git, all project files; in both cases excluding the project-root `book` and `evidence` directories, `.git` and `target` directories at any depth, and paths disallowed by {cite}`requirements.configuration.evidence_paths`. Evidence snapshots and generated build output MUST therefore not be counted as source references.
A source item MUST choose its references for each candidate definition by this
procedure, and MAY carry several:
1. If the item is a test or test helper designed to verify the definition, it
MUST use `{test}`.
2. Otherwise, if fulfilling the definition depends on the item, it MUST use
`{impl}`. For code, this means it makes a decision, performs a check,
produces an output, or handles a case the definition specifies. For a type,
this means the definition constrains its shape: fields, variants, serialized
form, or validation.
3. Otherwise, if the item should be re-checked or kept in sync when the
definition changes, it MUST use `{cite}`.
4. If the item carries no reference after applying steps 1 to 3 to every
definition, it MUST cite the built-in `habeas:none` under
{cite}`requirements.references.no_requirement`, justifying why the item
exists.
```text
{impl}`requirements.references.targets`
{cite}`requirements.references.targets`
{test}`requirements.references.targets`
:::{req} initial_prompt
The initial request MUST provide the six tool definitions above and the
following prompt. The harness MUST replace `{{subject_kind}}` with `requirement`
or `example`, `{{subject_name}}` with the full subject name, and
`{{mandatory_inputs}}` with the complete mandatory inputs as a JSON array using
the existing evidence-input formats. The template MUST otherwise be used as
written. Its review guidance MUST follow {impl}`requirements.ci.review_criteria`,
{cite}`requirements.examples.evidence`, and {cite}`requirements.ci.outcomes`.
```text
Bring your expert judgment to the task of assessing whether a project's sources satisfy a requirement or example.
Subject: {{subject_kind}} {{subject_name}}
Read the subject and mandatory inputs below. Use habeas to request any additional
source information you need. Use list_files to discover files and directories,
outline to list a file's selectable nodes, ripgrep to search file contents, and
references to list requirement names or
every source that references the selected definitions.
The harness records source inputs for you; listings and reference lookups are
not evidence.
Assess only the named subject, using cited requirements and definitions as context.
For a requirement, check that the code marked {impl} implements every obligation
completely and exactly as stated, and that tests cover the interesting points in
the design space, including relevant boundaries and failure cases. Also check that the
implementation is marked completely: code that implements part of the
requirement without an {impl} reference to it, including code that refers to it
only with {cite}, is a gap. So is behavior in the {impl} code that this
requirement does not specify, unless another definition that code implements
specifies it. When another requirement implements part of the subject, assess
whether its text carries out that part; do not reassess its implementation,
tests, or evidence. If there are no tests,
assess whether simplicity or impracticality justifies their absence, and explain.
For an example, assess whether test setup and assertions cover its scenario and
expected outcomes. A true judgment needs at least one {test} reference to the
example in the supplied inputs. Explain the coverage.
Choose true when the subject meets these criteria. Choose {"FIXME": ["..."]} when
the remaining gaps are explicitly acknowledged in source comments or tests;
list their issue references or other identifying content. The usual convention
is FIXME(#125) or FIXME(rust-lang/rust#123), but references may occur elsewhere.
Choose false for other gaps or insufficient evidence. Explain your judgment in
a Markdown rationale with source locations, including any acknowledged gaps; for
a requirement, explain the implementation and testing judgments.
When you are ready, call submit_judgment exactly once with determination and
rationale. That tool call is your final answer.
Mandatory inputs:
{{mandatory_inputs}}
